subject: Pricing metrics — tokens vs characters vs requests
messages:
From: Marissa Cole <marissa@redwood.example.com>

Cc: Dylan Brooks <dylan@redwood.example.com>

Subject: Post-call recap + clarification on pricing metrics

Hi Taylor / Samir —

Great to speak today — thanks for the time. Quick recap and two asks to make sure the pilot we sketch out has accurate cost estimates:

1) Recap of what I heard from the call:
- Primary use: contextual patient-summary generation for intake triage and clinician notes.
- Typical request: 1–2 long prompts (up to ~2k characters) + context window (patient history + prior notes) ~6k–8k characters.
- Peak volume: expected ~10k–20k requests/day after initial rollout; average likely lower.

2) Asks from our side to finalize pricing:
- Can you confirm the expected daily request count and typical context/prompt sizes? (approx characters or sample lengths is fine)
- Do you have a target budget in mind (ballpark $/month or $/1M tokens)? You mentioned wanting unit economics (target $/1M tokens) to compare with current vendor.

3) Pricing/metering note we discussed — we saw some confusion on the call between tokens, characters, and requests. For the estimate we typically use:
- Billing unit: billed tokens (not raw characters). We provide guidance to convert characters -> tokens (roughly ~4 characters per token for English typical text, but depends on encoding and punctuation).
- Requests: each API call is a request, but billing is per-billed-token (input + output). Requests are useful for concurrency/throughput planning, not direct cost.
- Prompt caching: caching reduces billed tokens only if the exact prefix and KV cache hit means the model does less work. We can apply prefix caching for static system prompts and stable templates; cached responses still incur some billed tokens for the returned text, but repeated identical token generation can be avoided with cached responses on Redwood's side (saves billed tokens).

I attached a quick token_estimate.xlsx that shows conversions and a few sample scenarios (low/med/high). If you can reply with approximate request counts and confirm budget range, I’ll run a tokenized cost model and propose a pilot (1–2 week) with a target $/1M tokens comparison and an expected monthly spend.

Thanks — cc'ing Dylan for a quick engineering note on caching/kv behavior.

Best,

Thanks Marissa — this is helpful. A few clarifications from our side: 

- Request volume: early rollout (month 1) ~3k requests/day; month 3 target ~15k requests/day. We expect burst concurrency but average will be closer to 8–10k/day after month 3.
- Prompt sizes: our system prompt + templates are stable and about 800–1,200 characters. Variable patient context averages ~4k characters. Output summary length target ~600–900 characters.
- Budget: we're looking at a target unit cost goal of $100–150 per 1M tokens (this is what our procurement team asked us to aim for). Right now our incumbent is in that ballpark but with less predictable latency.

We got tripped up on tokens vs characters vs requests during the call — can you confirm how you’ll calculate billed tokens? Example: if input is 5k characters and output 800 characters, what does that look like in tokens? Also curious how caching helps — if the system prompt is the same across requests, do we get billed for it every time?

Thanks Taylor — good details. Below is a concrete worked example and short notes on caching. Dylan added a technical footnote below.

Worked example (approx):
- Assumptions: 1 token ~= 4 characters (English average). This is a rule-of-thumb; exact tokenization varies by encoding/model.
- Input: total characters = 5,000 (system prompt + templates + patient context) -> estimated tokens = 5,000 / 4 = 1,250 tokens (input).
- Output: 800 characters -> ~200 tokens (output).
- Total billed tokens per request (input + output) ~= 1,450 tokens.

If you do 10,000 requests/day at 1,450 billed tokens/request -> 14.5M tokens/day -> ~435M tokens/month (30d). At $100 / 1M tokens, that would be $43,500/month. At $150 / 1M tokens, $65,250/month.

Key notes on caching and what affects billed tokens: 
- System prompts / static prefix caching: if the system prompt + template is identical between requests, Redwood can cache the prefix and avoid re-sending it to the model for repeated requests at inference time. That means the model runtime doesn't have to regenerate those tokens — you effectively avoid billed input tokens for the cached prefix. However:
  - If your patient context is unique per request (which it is), that part will still be billed.
  - If the output is deterministic and we cache full-response matches, repeated identical requests could return a cached response with zero model generation cost (and thus zero billed tokens for the generation), but in practice with patient-specific fields you rarely get full-response cache hits.
- KV-cache / generation mechanics: caching helps most when a large static system prompt contributes the majority of the input token count. If your system prompt is ~1k chars and patient context ~4k chars, caching reduces the billed tokens by removing that 1k-char prompt from the recurring input.

Next steps I’ll do:
- Run an exact tokenized pass if you can share a couple of redacted sample prompts (so we use real token counts instead of estimates).
- Produce a 3-scenario cost sheet (low/med/high) at $100 and $150 per 1M tokens and include an ROI row vs your incumbent.

Engineering note from Dylan (cc'd): please see the short note below re: prompt caching and billed tokens mechanics.

Best,
Marissa

From: Dylan Brooks <dylan@redwood.example.com>
Date: Sat, 29 Aug 2026 11:45:00 -0700
To: Taylor Burns <taylor@acmehealth.com>, Marissa Cole <marissa@redwood.example.com>
Subject: Re: engineering note — prompt caching/billed tokens

Quick tech detail:
- Tokenization: we use the same tokenizer as the model family; characters -> tokens conversion is only approximate. For cost modeling we do exact tokenization of samples you provide.
- Billed tokens: Redwood bills for model inference work (input + output tokens). If the prefix is cached server-side and we can avoid re-executing that part of the attention graph, the billed tokens for that prefix can be reduced. Practically:
  - Partial caching: we can store and reuse KV cache for the static prefix (system prompt + template) so that runtime cost for that prefix is removed; billed token reduction equals the token count of that prefix for cache hits.
  - Cache hit requirements: identical tokenized bytes for the cached prefix. Any change in punctuation/whitespace can change tokenization and reduce hit-rate.
  - Requests still have minimal overhead per call: metadata, routing, and response bytes are not billed as tokens but we monitor rate-limiting and quotas.

I attached token_estimate.xlsx with a sample tokenized scenario and a small formula tab to adjust the characters->token ratio. Also uploaded a small tool we can run with your redacted prompts to produce exact counts (link above).

Happy to jump on a short call with your engineering team to walk through the cache tradeoffs and pilot instrumentation.

—Dylan
